729.title: Moggallana's powers
729.hook: foremost in psychic power, and still humble
729.howItsDone: In Theravada communities Moggallana is honored with Sariputta as one of the Buddha's two chief disciples, and in some temples their images stand on either side of the Buddha.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sariputta, the general of the dhamma, and your line, wisdom explains. Today, the other friend of the pact, Kolita, now called Moggallana.

On the path down from Vulture Peak, the hill outside Rajagaha, Moggallana smiles. His companion on the walk, Lakkhana, notices and asks what any friend would ask: why the smile? And Moggallana, who in the texts could see things no one around him saw, doesn't answer. Not here, he says. Ask me again when we're with the Buddha. That small refusal on a dusty path is a good door into a man whose powers were famous. The texts care about what he could do. They seem to care even more about how he carried it.
screen: `A SMILE ON THE PATH.` → `WHY THE SMILE?` → `NOT HERE. ASK ME LATER.`

segments.voice: First, the reputation. In the Anguttara Nikaya's list of foremost disciples, the Buddha names Moggallana foremost in psychic power. Earlier on this path we watched him, in another discourse, shake a palace of the gods with his toe. Second, the smile explained. Later, before the Buddha, Lakkhana asks again, and now Moggallana tells it: on the path he saw a suffering being, a body of bones, tormented by birds as it moved through the air. And the Buddha backs him up. In paraphrase: I saw that being too, once, but I didn't speak of it. Others wouldn't have believed me, and that would have been to their harm. So the power is real in the story, and so is the restraint. Say it when it can help, and not before. Third, his slips. In a whole chapter of the Samyutta Nikaya, Moggallana tells his fellow monks how his own meditation went. He reached a deep stillness, and lost it. Distraction crept back in. And the Buddha, he says, came to him and said: Moggallana, don't be careless. Then the next stage, and the same thing again. He ends, in paraphrase: if anyone is a disciple who reached greatness with the teacher's help, it's me. The strongest one in the room, telling everyone where he kept falling. Fourth, the mirror. In the Majjhima Nikaya he teaches monks to check themselves the way someone looks in a mirror: seeing a smudge on their face, they wipe it off, and seeing none, they're glad. Power, in his hands, keeps turning back into honesty about himself.
screen: `FOREMOST IN PSYCHIC POWER.` · `A SMILE, AND A WAIT.` · `HE TELLS WHERE HE SLIPPED.` · `A MIRROR FOR YOUR OWN FACE.` · then, large: `POWER, HUMBLY.`

segments.voice: Name one thing you're good at, cooking, spreadsheets, calming a crying child, and let yourself admit it's real. Then, like Moggallana, recall one time that strength slipped, or someone helped you get it back, and hold both at once, the strength and the help, as you rest with the breath.
Moggallana's powers. Named foremost in psychic power, he holds back what he sees until it can help, tells where he slipped, and teaches the mirror. Today's word.

730.title: Like the earth
730.hook: accused of a slight, Sariputta says he is like the earth that bears all things without complaint (AN 9.11)
730.howItsDone: Monks and nuns in some Buddhist communities ask one another's forgiveness at set times, and Sariputta's earth image is taught as a model of patience under criticism.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Moggallana's powers, real and held with restraint, and your line, power, humbly. Today, back to Sariputta, on a bad day.

He hit me, and he left without a word of apology. That's the complaint, more or less. The rainy season is over at Savatthi, and Sariputta has just said goodbye to the Buddha and set out on the road. Behind him, a monk goes to the Buddha and says Sariputta struck him and walked off. The Buddha doesn't settle it himself. He sends for Sariputta. And word goes around the monastery that something worth hearing is about to happen. In the Anguttara Nikaya, this is Sariputta's lion's roar.
screen: `HE HIT ME AND LEFT.` → `THE BUDDHA SENDS FOR HIM.` → `A LION'S ROAR.`

segments.voice: First, what he doesn't say. Sariputta doesn't call the man a liar or list his own good deeds. He begins, in paraphrase: someone who wasn't mindful of the body might strike a fellow monk and walk away without apologizing. Then he describes his own mind with a picture. Second, the earth. People throw all kinds of things on the earth, he says, clean things and filthy things. Spit, blood, worse. And the earth isn't repelled, isn't ashamed, isn't disgusted. It just bears it. In the same way, he says, I live with a mind like the earth: wide, large, without hostility and without ill will. Third, more pictures. Water washes clean things and filthy things without turning away. Wind blows over all of it. A dusting cloth wipes up whatever it's given. Each image shows the same thing from another side: a mind that takes what comes without striking back. Fourth, the ending, and the surprising part. The monk who made the accusation falls at the Buddha's feet and admits he spoke falsely. The Buddha tells Sariputta to pardon him. And Sariputta says, in paraphrase: I pardon him, if he asks me to. And let him pardon me too. The one who was wronged asks to be forgiven as well. The Dhammapada uses the same picture for someone who has done the work: patient like the earth. Not a doormat, in this story. Sariputta speaks, clearly, in front of everyone. He just doesn't throw anything back.

731.title: Two deaths
731.hook: Sariputta goes home to teach his mother and dies; Moggallana is killed by bandits; the assembly seems empty (SN 47.14)
731.howItsDone: Relics said to be those of Sariputta and Moggallana are honored at some Buddhist sites, and the two disciples are remembered together in temples and at Buddhist festivals.

segments.voice: Yesterday: like the earth. Sariputta, accused, answered without throwing anything back. Today, the last day with the two friends.

A young novice named Cunda is walking to Savatthi with something that isn't his: a bowl and a robe. They belonged to Sariputta, his teacher. In the Samyutta Nikaya, Sariputta has fallen gravely ill in a village in Magadha, and with that illness he has passed away. Cunda carries the bowl and robe to Ananda, and Ananda brings him to the Buddha. That's how the news arrives: not with a speech, but with a monk's few belongings, carried by hand. Two friends once made a pact. Today, the texts let them go.
screen: `A NOVICE CARRIES A BOWL.` → `SARIPUTTA HAS DIED.` → `TWO FRIENDS, LET GO.`

segments.voice: First, Sariputta. The discourse says only that he was sick in a village of Magadha and died there. Later commentaries add a story. Tradition says he went back to the house where he was born, because his mother had never accepted the Buddha's teaching, and that in his last night he taught her and she understood. A son's last work, done at home. Second, Moggallana. Here too the discourses say little. A later story in the commentaries tells that he was attacked by bandits, hired by rivals of the Buddha's community, and killed. Tradition adds that he could have escaped, and in the end let it come. Third, the empty assembly. Not long after both had died, the Buddha is sitting in the open air at Ukkacela, on the bank of the Ganges, with a crowd of monks around him. He looks over them in silence. Then he says, in paraphrase: this assembly seems empty to me now. When those two were alive, it was not empty. Wherever they were staying, I had no worry about that place. Fourth, the tree. The Buddha goes on: how could anything that's born, made, bound to break, not break? It's as if the largest branches had fallen from a great tree that still stands, sound at the heart. The tree goes on. The branches are gone. And then the words heard earlier on this path: be islands to yourselves, with the dhamma as your refuge. Look back at the pair: a festival gone hollow, a pact, a verse passed on, the general, the powers, the earth, and today, two deaths.
screen: `SARIPUTTA, SICK, AT HOME.` · `MOGGALLANA, A LATER STORY.` · `THE ASSEMBLY SEEMS EMPTY.` · `BRANCHES OFF A GREAT TREE.` · then, large: `THE ASSEMBLY SEEMS EMPTY.`

732.title: Thus have I heard
732.hook: the cousin who remembered everything; most discourses begin with his words
732.carry: a letter with an address attached
732.howItsDone: When Buddhist discourses are chanted, in Pali in Theravada communities and in Chinese, Tibetan or Japanese in others, the chant often begins with the words 'thus have I heard' in that language.

segments.voice: Yesterday: two deaths, a bowl carried home and a great tree missing its branches. Your line, the assembly seems empty. Today, the one who stayed close at hand.

"Thus have I heard." Open the long discourses in the Victorian English of Rhys Davids, and those are the first words you meet. Turn the page to the next discourse, and there they are again. Then a place: at one time the Blessed One was staying near such-and-such a town, in such-and-such a grove. Then the teaching. The same small doorway, discourse after discourse. And the obvious question: who is the I? Who heard?
screen: `THUS HAVE I HEARD.` → `AGAIN, AND AGAIN.` → `WHO IS THE I?`

segments.voice: Tradition gives one answer: Ananda. He was, tradition says, the Buddha's cousin, and for a long stretch his personal attendant, close at hand when the Buddha taught. In the Anguttara Nikaya's list of foremost disciples, the qualities named for him include great learning and a good memory. So the I is the man who remembered. A story a few days from now tells how he came to say these words aloud for the whole community. Now look at what the phrase does. First, it's a witness, not an author. Not, I teach. Not even, the Buddha taught. Just: this is what I heard. The speaker steps aside and points to someone else. Second, it fixes the scene. After it comes where the Buddha was staying, and often who came to him and why. The teaching arrives with an address attached, like a letter. Third, it's honest about distance. Heard is a modest verb. It admits that what follows passed through one person's ears and memory. Some readers hear humility in it; others hear a claim of reliability: I was there. Both can be true at once. Fourth, it kept going. The opening shows up in sutras of later traditions too, in Sanskrit and Chinese, the Diamond Sutra among them. One person's careful listening became the front door of a library. And none of it would exist if someone hadn't paid attention in the room and kept what he heard without improving it.

Ananda. The one tradition credits as the witness behind every discourse's opening, thus have I heard, remembering what he heard, where, and from whom. Today's word.

733.title: Twenty-five years
733.hook: Ananda's decades as attendant, bringing water, keeping the door
733.carry: like a shadow that never leaves
733.howItsDone: In Buddhist monasteries, junior monks and nuns may attend their teachers, bringing water and food and caring for their needs, and Ananda is remembered as the model attendant.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ananda, the witness behind thus have I heard, and your line, a letter with an address attached. Today, what stood behind that remembering: years of showing up.

Some jobs leave no record but the person doing them. The cup is filled, the door is answered, the visitor waits the right amount of time, and none of it gets written down. Ananda's job was that kind. In the verses the Theragatha gives him, he does something unexpected. He counts. Not his insights, not his sermons: his years of service. Twenty-five of them, he says, at the Buddha's side. And he says what kind of years they were.
screen: `WORK THAT LEAVES NO RECORD.` → `HE COUNTS THE YEARS.` → `TWENTY-FIVE.`

segments.voice: First, the shadow. In paraphrase, Ananda says: for twenty-five years I attended the Blessed One with loving deeds, like a shadow that never leaves. Then he says it again for loving speech, and again for loving thoughts. Body, words, mind: service all the way through. Second, the water. In the long discourse on the Buddha's last journey, the old teacher is tired and thirsty by a little stream and asks Ananda for a drink. Ananda hesitates. Carts have just crossed, he says, and churned it up. There's a clear river not far on. The Buddha asks again, and again. So Ananda goes, bowl in hand, and finds the stream running clear. Even a devoted attendant sometimes has to be asked three times, and goes. Third, the night watch. In the Udana, the monks are gathered for their observance night. The Buddha sits in silence, and the night wears on. Late in the night Ananda gets up, arranges his robe, and says, in paraphrase: Lord, the night is far gone, the monks have been sitting a long time. Will you recite the rule for them? He's keeping time for everyone in the room. Fourth, the perks he turned down. The commentaries tell that when Ananda agreed to be attendant, he asked for conditions. Tradition says he asked not to be given the Buddha's robes or food, or a place in his lodging, so no one could say he served for the benefits. He asked instead to bring visitors to the Buddha, and to hear any teaching he'd missed. The service, by that story, was the whole point.
screen: `LIKE A SHADOW THAT NEVER LEAVES.` · `WATER FROM A CHURNED STREAM.` · `KEEPING TIME AT NIGHT.` · `NO PERKS, PLEASE.` · then, large: `TWENTY-FIVE YEARS.`

segments.voice: Think of one person you'll be around today and a small thing you could do for them that they may never notice: refill the water, clear the sink, hold a door. Twenty-five years. In his own verses, Ananda counts the years he attended the Buddha, in deed, word and thought, like a shadow that never leaves. Today's word.

734.title: Speaking for the women
734.hook: he asks the Buddha whether women can awaken, and the answer is yes (Vinaya, Cullavagga 10)
734.howItsDone: In Buddhist tradition Mahapajapati is remembered as the first nun, and Ananda as the one who spoke up for the women.

segments.voice: Yesterday: twenty-five years of Ananda's quiet service, and your line, like a shadow that never leaves. Today the attendant does something louder.

Early on this path, we stood outside a hall at Vesali with Mahapajapati and the women who had walked there, dusty and in tears, to ask to be ordained. We heard Ananda go in for them. Today we stay with Ananda: the exact question he asked, what came back, and what it cost him much later. The Vinaya, the monks' own rulebook, keeps all three. A request has been turned down three times. Ananda decides not to ask the same thing a fourth time. He asks something else.
screen: `BACK AT VESALI.` → `NO, THREE TIMES.` → `HE ASKS SOMETHING ELSE.`

segments.voice: First, the question. Ananda stops asking whether women may go forth, and asks whether they can. In paraphrase: Lord, if a woman goes forth into the homeless life, is she able to realize the fruits of the path, even full awakening? It's a question about ability, not permission. Second, the answer. Yes, Ananda. They are able. That yes is written into the Vinaya itself. Then Ananda speaks for one woman in particular. Mahapajapati, he reminds the Buddha, was the Buddha's own aunt and foster mother, who nursed him and fed him after his mother died. And the Buddha agrees to ordain women, with eight special rules. Third, the garland. Ananda carries the rules out to Mahapajapati, and she answers with a picture, in paraphrase: as a young person who has just bathed would take a garland of flowers in both hands and set it on their own head, so I take these rules. Buddhists today read that moment in different ways. Some hear grace in her acceptance. Others question the rules themselves and their history. Both readings are part of the conversation now. Fourth, the cost. After the Buddha's death, at a gathering of elders, Ananda is charged with faults, and one of them is that he worked to have women ordained. His answer, in paraphrase: I did it because Mahapajapati had nursed the Blessed One. I don't see it as a fault. But out of respect for you, I confess it. He confessed, and didn't pretend he had changed his mind. Speaking up for someone can be counted against you long after. The text keeps that too.

735.title: Water from the well
735.hook: a later story: Ananda asks an outcaste girl for water; she hesitates to give it; he says he asked for water, not her caste
735.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers tell the story of Ananda and the Matanga girl when teaching that birth and caste don't decide a person's worth, and it has been retold in later plays and dance.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Mahapajapati, and Ananda's question that got a yes. Your line, women can awaken. Today Ananda is the one who needs something, and asks a stranger.

Ananda is thirsty, and there's a well ahead, with a young woman drawing water. He asks her for a drink. Simple enough. Except she doesn't hand it over. She steps back and tells him what she is: a girl of the Matanga people, born outside the castes, the ones whose touch, in her world, was thought to make others unclean. She isn't being rude. She's protecting him, by the rules she's lived under all her life. And now he has to answer.
screen: `A THIRSTY MONK, A WELL.` → `HE ASKS FOR A DRINK.` → `SHE STEPS BACK.`

segments.voice: First, where this comes from. It's a later story, not from the Pali discourses. It's told in Sanskrit collections like the Divyavadana and in Buddhist texts preserved in Chinese, and the tellings give the young woman a name, Prakriti. Second, her refusal. She tells Ananda, in paraphrase: I'm a Matanga girl. I can't give you water. She expects her birth to end the conversation. Third, his answer, the line the story is remembered for. In paraphrase: sister, I didn't ask about your caste or your family. If you have water to spare, give it to me, and I'll drink. He doesn't give a lecture on equality. He just won't let her birth come between a thirsty man and a cup of water. So she gives it, and he drinks. Fourth, where the story goes next. Later tellings carry it a long way: she falls in love with the monk who spoke to her like that, there's trouble, a spell, the Buddha steps in, and in the end she asks to join the community and becomes a nun. The details differ from telling to telling. The heart of it doesn't. Earlier on this path the Buddha said that no one is an outcast by birth, only by what they do. Here the same idea shows up in a cup of water. This week ran from Moggallana's powers, like the earth, two deaths, Ananda, twenty-five years and speaking for the women, to today's water from the well.
